# Magga Saṁyutta (SN 45)

**ID:** SN 45
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Magga Saṁyutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0305m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Maggasaṁyutta* (SN 45), the opening section of the *Mahāvagga* of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, is dedicated to the Noble Eightfold Path (*ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga*), the foundational "middle way" in Buddhist practice [Norman 1983]. While cataloged as containing 180 discourses, much of its numerical extent consists of formulaic repetition series (*peyyāla*), including the *Gaṅgā-peyyāla*, *Appamāda-*, *Balakaraṇīya-*, *Esanā-*, and *Ogha-vagga* (S V 38–62) [Gethin 2001]. The commentary (*Sāratthappakāsinī*) and manuscript colophons establish that these repetition series in the *Maggasaṁyutta* provide the structural and stylistic template expanded in subsequent *saṁyuttas* of the *Mahāvagga*, such as the *Bojjhaṅga-*, *Indriya-*, and *Jhānasaṁyutta* (*yathā Maggasamyuttaṁ evaṁ...*) [Norman 1983; Gethin 2001].

The collection defines the eight path factors systematically, beginning with right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), explained as direct knowledge of the Four Noble Truths, progressing through virtue and mental training, and culminating in right immersion (*sammāsamādhi*) and the four *jhānas* [Anderson 1999]. A central doctrinal discourse is the *Magga-vibhaṅga Sutta* (SN 45.8), which details each step of the path, including the components of right speech and right view [Anderson 1999; Pa Auk Sayadaw et al. 2009]. Another celebrated discourse is the *Upaḍḍhasutta* (SN 45.2), in which the Buddha corrects Ānanda's assertion that good companionship is half of the spiritual life, declaring instead that admirable friendship (*kalyāṇamittatā*) constitutes the entirety of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) [Global Recovery 2010]. Other discourses employ similes, such as the diverse winds blowing across the sky, to illustrate how the path brings the four establishments of mindfulness to fulfillment [Gethin 2001].

 Additional parallels exist in the Tibetan Kangyur (D 300, *Kalyāṇa-mitra-sevana-sūtra* to SN 45.2), the *Madhyama Āgama* (MĀ 141), and the Sanskrit *Arthaviniścayasūtra*.
